title: Senator Unveils Bill to Force More Disclosure of Deaths in ICE Custody
author: Philip Wang
body:
As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress next year, Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey on Thursday unveiled new legislation aimed at addressing the surge in deaths of people in immigration detention centers.

The Death in Detention Transparency Act put forward by Kim would beef up what Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is required to tell Congress when a detainee dies in a detention center, hospital, or while being transported. Lawmakers and activists have complained that the Trump Administration has dragged its feet on making such notifications, and provided scant details about the conditions under which dozens of people have died.

“We cannot allow ICE and CBP to skirt accountability for their abuses at detention facilities around the country,” Kim said. “We cannot allow them to try to cover up how many people have died under their watch.”

The bill would cut the timeline from 90 days to 30 days when ICE has to make a report on a detainee death public, and would also require ICE disclose any deaths that happened during an enforcement operation, such as an arrest or a traffic stop.

Details regarding the death, including a copy of the results of an independent autopsy, and information such whether a firearm was discharged and if there is any relevant body camera footage, would also need to be included in the public report.

Private contractors, which run most of the ICE detention facilities, need to abide by death reporting requirements when agreeing to run detention facilities for the agency. Failure to comply on more than three occasions would subject a contractor to a five-year suspension of operations, along with other enforcement measures, according to the bill.

Kim’s office said the legislation is in response to the death of three detainees in less than eight months from Delaney Hall in New Jersey, a privately-owned facility run by GEO Group that was plagued with allegations of unsanitary living conditions and medical neglect. ICE has refused to disclose details of the third death, saying only that the detainee experienced a “medical emergency” and was released from ICE’s custody to a local hospital. The agency in June stopped reporting the deaths of those detainees who had been released from federal custody, claiming that it is not responsible for “monitoring or reviewing deaths that may occur.”

Kim, a member of the Senate Homeland Security Committee who has visited the Delaney Hall facility multiple times, says the bill would help to ensure no family is left in the dark about what is happening to their loved ones in the detention facilities.

The Senate bill comes on the heels of New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport suing the Department of Homeland Security on Tuesday to compel information regarding the medical care provided inside Delaney Hall and whether they were properly licensed. The state government is also seeking records of what happened when detainees sought treatment and documentation of injuries, deaths and emergency hospital visits. Davenport’s suit came after GEO Group declined to cooperate with New Jersey’s investigation into the facility, arguing that the records were federal documents and the state needed to go through the Department of Homeland Security for access.

Delaney Hall has also become a flashpoint for protests and clashes over congressional oversight. In May, Kim was pepper sprayed by federal agents outside the facility as he tried to defuse a confrontation with demonstrators. A year earlier, Rep. LaMonica McIver of New Jersey was indicted on charges of forcibly impeding and interfering with federal officers during an oversight visit. She disputed the allegations and called the prosecution politically motivated.

The number of deaths in ICE detention centers has been on the rise nationwide. ICE has so far reported 29 detention deaths in 2026, second only to the 33 recorded in 2025. A sizable portion of the deaths in ICE detention centers are a result of medical neglect. The agency’s own internal investigators said that staff members at the detention facilities “deviated from safe limits of practice” or “did not provide medical care within safe limits of practice” in at least 23 of the 33 deaths reported in 2025, according to records obtained by the San Francisco Chronicle. The investigator also said medical staff failed to perform CPR correctly or at all on immigrant detainees who then died in eight different instances.

The Trump administration has downplayed the rising number of deaths, arguing that the death tolls are proportional to the massive expansion of the detained population. In an interview with CBS News in May, White House border czar Tom Homan defended ICE’s practices, saying that the death rate among ICE’s detention centers are “far below” any state prisons and federal prisons, and that ICE is providing initial medical screenings to detainees who “have never seen a doctor before.”

As Democrats are projected to gain majorities of both chambers in Congress, House and Senate Democrats are teeing up legislation aiming to overhaul the immigration system and ICE’s practice. It’s unclear how much appetite the new Democratic majority will have for working to pass such measures, especially as President Trump has vowed to use this veto power often once Democrats take over Congress.
